name: Tulu
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Tulu is not in the catalog. The single title hit, Radhakrishna 2005 'Tulu Prosody: A critical study' (Kannur Univ. Ph.D., Kannada), was fetched sources in full from Shodhganga (hdl 10603/110069) and read from page images: it is a study of verse metre (chandas), silent on word stress; its section 3.10 'ಸ್ಟ್ ಎಂಬ ಧ್ವನಿಮಾ' concerns the Old-Tulu alveolar consonant 'sṭ', not stress. Two further open Shodhganga theses were fetched sources and read: Rama 1978 'Structural Description of Tulu' (Kerala; = Glottolog's Rama 2017 Kasaragod Tulu) has a 'Stress' section (p. 85) treating stress only as normal-vs-emphatic vocal qualifiers with no placement rule, and Kekunnaya 1990 'Comparative Study of Tulu Dialects' (Mangalore) has no suprasegmental section at all. The best first-hand statements remain Ramaswami Aiyar 1936 p. 411 (accent on the root = initial root syllable of native words, weak, stress-plus-pitch) and 1932 pp. 906-907 (primary accent generally on the root syllable), both read from saved page images. Unread and worth acquiring: Shetty 2001 Comprehensive Grammar of Tulu (high; secondary citation says first syllable usually stressed), Bhat 1967 and Bhatt 1971 (medium; snippets only, HathiTrust search-only). All fetched sources

earlier_scan.source_named: Bhat, D.N.S. 1967. Descriptive Analysis of Tulu (Deccan College); also Bhat 1998 'Tulu' in Steever (ed.) The Dravidian Languages — not online; Brigel 1872 grammar (read on archive.org) has no accent statement

new_statements.quote: (1) The relationship between dynamic stress and 'musical' pitch in the south Dravidian speeches requires to be experimentally investigated. So far as I can see, accent in these speeches is constituted of both elements. The accent-marks (strong, medium,) given in this essay only symbolise a perceptible rise in stress or in pitch. Generally speaking, accent falls on the root-syllables of native words when separately uttered. In connected speech, two degrees of accent may be demarcated thus roughly: the strong accent which falls on the initial root syllables of important words of each breath-group, and a less strong accent on the root-syllables of other emphatic words in the breath-group.
new_statements.citation: Ramaswami Aiyar, L. V. 1936. Materials for a Sketch of Tulu Phonology. Indian Linguistics 6 (Grierson Commemoration Volume): 385-439 (Glottolog cites the 1963 reprint as pp. 84-126). Linguistic Society of India.
new_statements.locator: p. 411 (PDF page 432 of the archive.org scan in.ernet.dli.2015.46264), 'Short notes regarding the sounds', note (1); the accent-mark convention is on p. 410 fn. (1)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent (a mix of stress and pitch, weak by the author's own acoustic impression) falls on the root syllable of native words, which in Tulu/Dravidian is the word-initial syllable; the author himself says 'initial root syllables'. An equally faithful label would be morphological-root, but since Dravidian roots are word-initial the two coincide. Nothing is said about contrastiveness; the companion 1932 text (BSOS 6: 906 n.1, 907) says 'so far as single words of two or more syllables are concerned, the primary accent generally falls on the root-syllable' and that the nature of the accent (dynamic stress vs pitch) is undetermined.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Phrase-level only: 'a less strong accent on the root-syllables of other emphatic words in the breath-group'. In the transcribed texts a bar above marks primary and a bar below secondary accent (p. 410 fn. 1; 1932: 907), but no word-internal secondary-stress rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Exclamations/statements of strong feeling: 'pitch or intonation completely submerges the stress element' (p. 411). Grammatical accent on endings: [ʌ] 'in unaccented syllables has the value of [a]; but sometimes when for certain grammatical differentiations, [ʌ] has to receive a little stress or accent' e.g. 2pl. vs 3pl. tense endings (p. 412). Sentence accent is 'governed by the psychological importance of the particular word' (1932: 907).
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly distinguishes single words 'when separately uttered' (citation form) from connected speech / breath-groups (sentence accent). Accent described as perceptible rise in stress or pitch, 'far less strong' than Hindi stress (1932: 906 n.1).
new_statements.identity_note: Ramaswami Aiyar's data are Tulu of the Udipi / South Kanara area (informants such as Sridhar Sarma of Udipi), covering both the Brahmins' (Shivalli) dialect and the common 'folk-speech'; the 1936 remark is made for 'these passages' generally, not for one dialect. No separate Glottolog dialect code; the language-level code tulu1258 applies.

new_statements.quote: Generally speaking, accent falls on the root-syllables of native words when separately uttered. In connected speech, two degrees of accent may be demarcated thus roughly: the strong accent which falls on the initial root syllables of important words of each breath-group, and a less strong accent on the root-syllables of other emphatic words in the breath-group. Statements or exclamations expressive of strong feelings of course involve different degrees and varieties of accent in which pitch or intonation completely submerges the stress element.
new_statements.citation: Ramaswami Aiyar, L. V. 1936. Materials for a Sketch of Tulu Phonology. Indian Linguistics 6 (Grierson Commemoration Volume): 385-439; corroborated by Ramaswami Aiyar 1932, BSOS 6(4): 906 n.1-907.
new_statements.locator: p. 411, 'Short notes regarding the sounds', note (1) (= PDF page 432 of the DLI scan in.ernet.dli.2015.46264)
new_statements.reading: Word accent in Tulu falls on the root syllable, which the author identifies as the initial (root) syllable of native words; it is a weak accent made of both stress and pitch (the 1932 footnote adds that the primary accent 'generally falls on the root-syllable' of polysyllabic words and that its dynamic-vs-tonal nature is undetermined). Reads as fixed initial stress, impressionistic, with sentence-level prominence governed by pragmatic importance. Nothing read in this sweep gives a placement rule that is more explicit or more recent; Shetty 2001 (unread) reportedly says 'first syllable is usually stressed'.

sources.citation: Radhakrishna, N. 2005. Tulu Prosody: A Critical Study [Kannada title: ತುಳು ಛಂದಸ್ಸಿನ ವಿಮರ್ಶಾತ್ಮಕ ಅಧ್ಯಯನ, 'A critical study of Tulu metre']. Ph.D. thesis, Kannur University, School of Indian Languages, Govt. College Campus, Kasaragod (guide P. Srikrishna Bhat). 159 pp., in Kannada.
sources.quote: ಸಾಮಾನ್ಯವಾಗಿ ದೇಸೀ ಕಾವ್ಯಗಳನ್ನು ತಾರ ಸ್ವರಸ್ಥಾಯಿಯಲ್ಲಿ ಸ್ವರಾಘಾತಗಳೊಂದಿಗೆ ಹಾಡಲಾಗುತ್ತದೆ. ಸ್ವರಾಘಾತಗಳು ತಾಳದೊಂದಿಗೆ ತಾದಾತ್ಮ್ಯ ಹೊಂದುವ ಬದಲು ಅರ್ಥದೊಂದಿಗೆ ಸಂಬಂಧ ಹೊಂದಿರುತ್ತವೆ. (ch.6, p.146, point 30) [Folk poems are generally sung in a high pitch register with accents; the accents are tied to meaning rather than coinciding with the beat.]
sources.locator: Contents page; ch.1 pp.2-6; ch.3 sec.3.10 pp.53-55 and sec.3.11 pp.55-59; ch.6 p.146 point 30
sources.note: The work is 'prosody' in the Indian sense: chandas = verse metre (aksharagana, matragana, amsagana, yati/prasa, syllable weight fixed by the tala of sung recitation). The table of contents has no section on word stress; the abbreviations list only metrical treatises (Kannada Chandassu, Chandombudhi, Dravida Chandassu, Vrittamanjari...). Section 3.10 'ಸ್ಟ್ ಎಂಬ ಧ್ವನಿಮಾ' is about the Old-Tulu alveolar consonant phoneme written 'sṭ' (= Malayalam ṟṟ), not stress. The only accent remark (p.146) concerns pitch accents in sung folk verse tied to meaning. Silent on where word stress falls. Text layer…

sources.citation: Rama, M. 1978. Structural Description of Tulu. Ph.D. thesis (Linguistics), University of Kerala (guide V. I. Subramoniam). 575 pp. [Kasaragod Tulu; the 2017 printing 'Structural description of Kasaragod Tulu' is the Glottolog descriptive reference held in print at Harvard.]
sources.quote: Loudness and force of the speech are known as vocal qualifiers. In this dialect we notice two kinds of vocal qualifiers i.e. primary and secondary. The usual talk with normal speed is always identified as primary vocal qualifier. The extra-ordinary talk like extra short and extra long which are responsible in the meaning change of a particular speech, and exclamation come under secondary vocal qualifier. The usage of secondary vocal qualifier is very limited. [...] But within a word either one of these will occur.
sources.locator: ch. 1 Phonology, sec. 1.6 Suprasegmental Phonemes (thesis p. 84) and sec. 1.6.2 Stress (thesis p. 85) = pdf pages 31-32 of
sources.note: Treats 'stress' as expressive vocal qualifiers (normal vs emphatic), phonemic together with juncture, pitch (4 levels) and intonation; gives no rule of word-stress position. In its examples the primary mark sits on the first syllable of most words (àaye bàtte 'he came'; ònji, òri, ìtte) but on a non-initial syllable in uurùdu, aràse, naràmaani. Silent on a placement rule.

sources.note: p. 906 n.1 - 907 (verified on page images): 'Word-accent and sentence-accent exist in the enunciation of Tuḷu, as in the other south Dravidian speeches, though the precise character of this accent (i.e. whether it is dynamic stress or tonal pitch or a combination of the two) remains to be determined... So far as single words of two or more syllables are concerned, the primary accent generally falls on the root-syllable.' Accent 'far less strong' than Hindi stress; sentence accent governed by 'psychological importance'.
